insights.body: The disease called leprosy in English Bibles (Hebrew tsara'at) covered a range of skin conditions, not only Hansen's disease. It made a person ritually unclean and excluded from the temple, so Uzziah lived "in a separate house" while Jotham governed (26:21). In 1931 a stone plaque was found in Jerusalem, from the Second Temple period, saying that Uzziah's bones had been brought there and should not be opened.

insights.title: In the year Uzziah died
insights.body: The Chronicler says Isaiah wrote Uzziah's acts (26:22). Isaiah's vision of the holy King in the temple came "in the year that King Uzziah died." A king who entered the temple in pride and was struck down stands behind a prophet who entered in vision and cried, "Woe is me."

insights.title: When strength becomes danger
insights.body: Uzziah was "marvelously helped until he was strong" (26:15), and strength became the occasion of his fall. Why are success and security often more dangerous to faith than hardship?

27.summary: Jotham reigns sixteen years, building in Jerusalem and Judah and subduing the Ammonites, and grows strong because he ordered his ways before Yahweh.
27.lookfor: Notice what Jotham avoids doing, and what the chapter says about the people.

names.name: Jotham
names.gloss: Uzziah's son, king of Judah for sixteen years.

names.name: Zadok
names.gloss: Father of Jotham's mother, Jerushah; perhaps from the priestly family.

names.name: Ophel
names.gloss: The hill between the City of David and the temple mount in Jerusalem.

names.name: Ammon
names.gloss: A kingdom east of the Jordan with its capital at Rabbah, modern Amman.

names.name: Ahaz
names.gloss: Jotham's son and successor.

insights.title: A short, good reign
insights.body: Jotham's reign gets only nine verses, with no serious failures recorded. He did right as Uzziah had, "however he didn't enter into Yahweh's temple" (27:2), that is, he did not repeat his father's sin. He is one of the few kings of Judah whom Chronicles does not criticise.

insights.title: The people still corrupt
insights.body: "The people still acted corruptly" (27:2). A good king could not by himself turn the nation. The prophets active in this period, Isaiah, Hosea and Micah, describe the injustice and idolatry of the time.

insights.title: Building on Ophel
insights.body: Jotham built the upper gate of the temple and "much on the wall of Ophel" (27:3). Ophel, the ridge between the City of David and the temple mount, needed strong walls. Archaeologists have uncovered fortifications on Ophel from the period of Judah's kings.

insights.title: He ordered his ways
insights.body: Jotham "became mighty, because he ordered his ways before Yahweh his God" (27:6). The Hebrew verb kun means to make firm or establish. He set his course steadily before God, and God established his kingdom.

insights.title: Tribute from Ammon
insights.body: The Ammonites paid a hundred talents of silver and ten thousand cors each of wheat and barley for three years (27:5). Tribute in grain was common in the ancient world. The payments may have stopped when Assyria began to dominate the region.

insights.title: Clouds gathering
insights.body: Kings notes that in Jotham's days God began to send Rezin of Syria and Pekah of Israel against Judah. Chronicles leaves that out, but the threat breaks over his son Ahaz in the next chapter. Behind both, Assyria's power was rising.

28.summary: Ahaz worships Baal and sacrifices his children, Judah suffers crushing defeats by Syria and Israel, the northern prophet Oded persuades Israel to release its captives, and Ahaz turns to Assyria and other gods and shuts the temple doors.
28.lookfor: Notice the surprising kindness of the northerners toward their captives, and what Ahaz does with the temple.

names.name: Ahaz
names.gloss: King of Judah for sixteen years, one of its worst kings.

names.name: valley of the son of Hinnom
names.gloss: A valley south of Jerusalem where children were sacrificed; its name later gave Gehenna.

names.name: Pekah
names.gloss: King of Israel, son of Remaliah, allied with Syria against Judah.

names.name: Oded
names.gloss: A prophet in Samaria who urged the release of captives from Judah.

names.name: Jericho
names.gloss: The city of palm trees in the Jordan valley, near the border of Judah.

names.name: Tilgath Pilneser
names.gloss: Tiglath-pileser III, king of Assyria, to whom Ahaz appealed.

insights.title: Children in the fire
insights.body: Ahaz "burned his children in the fire, according to the abominations of the nations" (28:3). The Law strictly forbade child sacrifice. The valley of Hinnom where it happened later gave its name, Gehenna, to the place of final judgment in Jewish and Christian thought.

insights.title: The Syro-Ephraimite war
insights.body: Syria and Israel attacked Judah (28:5-6), probably to force it into their coalition against Assyria around 734 BC. Isaiah urged Ahaz to trust God rather than Assyria and gave him the sign of Immanuel. Ahaz refused and appealed to the Assyrian king.

insights.title: A prophet in Samaria
insights.body: Oded, a prophet of Yahweh in the northern kingdom, rebuked the victorious army: "Aren't there even with you trespasses of your own against Yahweh your God?" (28:10). Some northern leaders agreed and refused to keep the captives (28:12-13). The Chronicler, who rarely praises the north, holds them up as an example.

insights.title: A Samaritan kindness
insights.body: The northerners clothed, fed and anointed the captives, put the weak on donkeys and brought them to Jericho, to their brothers (28:15). Many scholars think Jesus' parable of the good Samaritan, with its road to Jericho, oil, wine and donkey, deliberately echoes this story. In both, mercy comes from the people Judah least expected.

insights.title: Trouble, not strength
insights.body: Tiglath-pileser "came to him, and gave him trouble, but didn't strengthen him" (28:20). The verb chazaq, to strengthen, is the root of Hezekiah's name, which means Yahweh strengthens, and recurs in his story. Ahaz sought strength from Assyria and received only distress.

insights.title: Distress makes him worse
insights.body: "In the time of his distress, he trespassed yet more against Yahweh, this same king Ahaz" (28:22). He sacrificed to the gods of Damascus because they seemed to have helped his enemies (28:23). Manasseh, by contrast, humbled himself when in distress.

insights.title: Doors shut
insights.body: Ahaz cut up the temple vessels and "shut up the doors of Yahweh's house" (28:24), building altars on every corner of Jerusalem instead. He comes close to undoing everything David and Solomon established. The first act of his son Hezekiah will be to open those doors again.

insights.title: Mercy from the enemy
insights.body: The captors who had just slaughtered Judah's soldiers listened to a prophet and showed tender care to their captives. What does this episode suggest about the possibility of repentance, even in the middle of conflict?

29.summary: In the first month of his reign Hezekiah reopens the temple, has the priests and Levites cleanse it, and restores sacrifices and Levitical music with great rejoicing.
29.lookfor: Notice how quickly Hezekiah acts, who proves more ready than the priests, and how sacrifice and song are joined.

names.name: Hezekiah
names.gloss: Ahaz's son, king of Judah for twenty-nine years and one of its greatest reformers.

names.name: Kidron
names.gloss: The valley east of Jerusalem where impure objects were taken and destroyed.

names.name: Gad
names.gloss: A prophet called David's seer.

names.name: Nathan
names.gloss: The prophet at David's court.

names.name: Asaph
names.gloss: A Levite singer of David's time, here called a seer; twelve psalms bear his name.

insights.title: Doors opened
insights.body: "In the first year of his reign, in the first month, he opened the doors of Yahweh's house" (29:3). Ahaz had shut them; Hezekiah's first act reverses that. Chronicles gives Hezekiah four chapters, mostly about worship, where Kings focuses on the Assyrian crisis.

insights.title: Like David
insights.body: Hezekiah did right "according to all that David his father had done" (29:2). Few kings receive such full praise. The Chronicler also presents him as a new Solomon, restoring the temple and celebrating feasts unmatched since Solomon's day.

insights.title: Sixteen days of cleansing
insights.body: Priests carried the uncleanness out of the inner sanctuary to the court, and Levites took it to the Kidron (29:16). The work took eight days for the courts and eight for the house (29:17). Only priests could enter the inner rooms, so the two groups worked in relay.

insights.title: Hands on the goats
insights.body: The king and assembly laid their hands on the goats for the sin offering (29:23), identifying with the animals offered for their sin. The sacrifice was "for all Israel" (29:24), including the north. Laying on of hands is prescribed for sin offerings and on the Day of Atonement.

insights.title: Yahweh's song
insights.body: "When the burnt offering began, Yahweh's song also began" (29:27). The Levites sang "with the words of David, and of Asaph the seer" (29:30), that is, psalms. David's musical order is said to have come "from Yahweh by his prophets" (29:25), giving it the same authority as the law of sacrifice.

insights.title: Levites more upright
insights.body: The priests were too few to flay all the offerings, so the Levites helped, "for the Levites were more upright in heart to sanctify themselves than the priests" (29:34). The Chronicler is willing to criticise the priests. Eagerness of heart counted for more than rank.

insights.title: Done suddenly
insights.body: "Hezekiah and all the people rejoiced, because of that which God had prepared for the people; for the thing was done suddenly" (29:36). The speed of the renewal is credited to God's preparation. After the darkness of Ahaz's reign, joy returns to the temple.

30.summary: Hezekiah invites all Israel, including the remnant in the north, to a Passover in Jerusalem, many come despite mockery, God pardons those who seek him though ritually unclean, and the festival is extended with great joy.
30.lookfor: Count how often the word turn or return appears in the letter, and notice how Hezekiah handles worshippers who are not ritually clean.

names.name: Ephraim
names.gloss: The leading tribe of the former northern kingdom.

names.name: Manasseh
names.gloss: A northern tribe, divided between both sides of the Jordan.

names.name: Zebulun
names.gloss: A northern tribe in Galilee.

names.name: Asher
names.gloss: A northern tribe along the coast north of Mount Carmel.

names.name: Issachar
names.gloss: A northern tribe near the Jezreel Valley.

insights.title: An invitation to the north
insights.body: Hezekiah wrote to Ephraim and Manasseh inviting them to Passover in Jerusalem (30:1). The northern kingdom had fallen to Assyria, and the letter addresses "the remnant of you that have escaped out of the hand of the kings of Assyria" (30:6). For the Chronicler, the fall of Samaria opened a door to reunite Israel around the temple.

insights.title: Passover in the second month
insights.body: They kept Passover in the second month because too few priests were ready and the people had not gathered (30:2-3). The Law allowed a second-month Passover for those unclean or far away. Hezekiah applied this provision to the whole nation.

insights.title: Turn and return
insights.body: The letter plays on the Hebrew shuv, to turn or return: "turn again to Yahweh... that he may return to the remnant" and "if you return to him" (30:6, 30:9). It promises that if Israel turns back, their exiled relatives may return to the land. It grounds the call in God's character: "gracious and merciful" (30:9).

insights.title: Mocked, yet some came
insights.body: Couriers passing through the north were ridiculed and mocked (30:10). "Nevertheless some men of Asher and Manasseh and of Zebulun humbled themselves, and came" (30:11). The pattern of mixed response to God's invitation recurs in Jesus' parable of the great banquet.

insights.title: Pardon for the heart
insights.body: Many northerners ate the Passover without proper cleansing, and Hezekiah prayed, "May the good Yahweh pardon everyone who sets his heart to seek God... even if they aren't clean according to the purification of the sanctuary" (30:18-19). "Yahweh listened to Hezekiah, and healed the people" (30:20). The verb heal recalls God's promise in 7:14, and the story puts the seeking heart above ritual exactness.

insights.title: Nothing like it since Solomon
insights.body: The festival was extended another seven days, as at Solomon's temple dedication, and "since the time of Solomon... there was nothing like this in Jerusalem" (30:26). Israelites from the north and resident foreigners joined in (30:25). For a moment the united kingdom of David and Solomon seemed restored.

insights.title: Ritual and the heart
insights.body: Hezekiah did not turn away eager but unclean worshippers, and God honoured his prayer. How do you weigh the importance of doing things rightly against welcoming those who come with a seeking heart?

31.summary: After the Passover the people destroy idolatrous shrines throughout the land, Hezekiah organises the priests and Levites, and the people bring tithes and offerings in such abundance that storerooms must be prepared.
31.lookfor: Notice how the people respond to the call to support the priests and Levites, and how the surplus is managed.

names.name: Asherah
names.gloss: Wooden poles or images linked with the goddess Asherah.

names.name: Azariah
names.gloss: The chief priest of the house of Zadok in Hezekiah's day.

names.name: Conaniah
names.gloss: The Levite in charge of the temple storerooms.

names.name: Kore
names.gloss: The Levite gatekeeper of the east gate, in charge of freewill offerings.

skim.advice: Read verses 1 to 10 and 20 to 21 closely. The lists of Levite officials and the details of distribution in verses 12 to 19 can be skimmed.

insights.title: Worship leads to reform
insights.body: When the Passover was over, the people went out and destroyed pillars, Asherah poles and high places, even in Ephraim and Manasseh (31:1). The reform came from the worshippers themselves, not only from royal command. Kings records Hezekiah's removal of the high places and of Moses' bronze serpent.

insights.title: Heaps from spring to autumn
insights.body: The people began piling up their offerings in the third month and finished in the seventh (31:7). That span runs from the grain harvest at the Feast of Weeks to the fruit and olive harvest at the Feast of Tents. The heaps grew with each harvest.

insights.title: Enough and plenty left over
insights.body: Azariah reports, "we have eaten and had enough, and have plenty left over, for Yahweh has blessed his people" (31:10). The Levites could "give themselves to Yahweh's law" (31:4) because they were supported. Malachi later called on the returned community to bring the full tithe into the storehouse.

insights.title: Yahweh's camp
insights.body: The priests and Levites served "in the gates of Yahweh's camp" (31:2). The phrase recalls the wilderness, when the Levites camped around the tabernacle. The Chronicler presents the temple as continuous with the camp of Israel in Moses' day.

insights.title: Rolls for the families
insights.body: Portions were distributed by genealogical lists that included males from three years old, and the wives and children of the Levites (31:16-18). Whole families were supported, not just those on duty. Accurate records ensured that none were overlooked.

insights.title: With all his heart
insights.body: Hezekiah "did that which was good, right, and faithful before Yahweh" and in every work he sought God "with all his heart, and prospered" (31:20-21). This verdict sums up the Chronicler's ideal king. The next chapter tests that faithfulness with Assyria's invasion.

32.summary: Sennacherib of Assyria invades Judah, Hezekiah fortifies Jerusalem, secures its water and encourages the people, and when he and Isaiah pray, God destroys the Assyrian army; later Hezekiah's pride and the visit of Babylonian envoys test his heart.
32.lookfor: Listen to the competing claims about whom to trust, and notice how the Chronicler summarises events that Kings and Isaiah tell at length.

names.name: Sennacherib
names.gloss: King of Assyria 705 to 681 BC, who invaded Judah in 701 BC.

names.name: Millo
names.gloss: A terraced structure in the City of David supporting buildings on the slope.

names.name: Lachish
names.gloss: Judah's second city, besieged and captured by Sennacherib.

names.name: Isaiah
names.gloss: The prophet, son of Amoz, who counselled Hezekiah during the Assyrian crisis.

names.name: Gihon
names.gloss: The spring just east of the City of David, Jerusalem's main water source.

insights.title: After this faithfulness
insights.body: "After these things and this faithfulness, Sennacherib king of Assyria came" (32:1). The Chronicler does not say faithfulness prevents trouble. It prepared Hezekiah to face it with trust. Kings adds that Hezekiah first paid a heavy tribute, which Chronicles leaves out.

insights.title: Hezekiah's tunnel
insights.body: Hezekiah "stopped the upper spring of the waters of Gihon, and brought them straight down on the west side of David's city" (32:30). A tunnel over 500 metres long, cut through rock from the Gihon spring to the Pool of Siloam, still exists. An inscription found in it in 1880 describes the two teams of diggers meeting in the middle.

insights.title: The broad wall
insights.body: Hezekiah rebuilt broken walls and built "the other wall outside" (32:5). Archaeologists in Jerusalem's Jewish Quarter have uncovered a wall about seven metres thick from this period, often called the Broad Wall. It enclosed a western quarter that had grown, perhaps with refugees from the fallen north.

insights.title: An arm of flesh
insights.body: "An arm of flesh is with him, but Yahweh our God is with us" (32:8). The arm was a picture of strength, and flesh stands for human weakness. Jeremiah curses the one who makes flesh his arm and blesses the one who trusts in Yahweh.

insights.title: Sennacherib's own account
insights.body: Sennacherib's annals, preserved on clay prisms, boast that he shut Hezekiah up in Jerusalem like a caged bird and took many Judean towns, but they do not claim the city was captured. Reliefs from his palace at Nineveh show the siege of Lachish (32:9). Kings and Isaiah tell of the angel striking the Assyrian camp in more detail.

insights.title: Killed in his god's house
insights.body: Sennacherib returned home in shame, and "when he had come into the house of his god, those who came out of his own bowels killed him" (32:21). Babylonian and Assyrian sources confirm he was murdered by a son, in 681 BC, twenty years after the campaign. The irony is sharp: the god he trusted could not protect him in its own temple.

insights.title: Pride and testing
insights.body: After his healing, Hezekiah's "heart was lifted up" (32:25), but he humbled himself (32:26). When Babylonian envoys came, "God left him, to try him, that he might know all that was in his heart" (32:31). Isaiah tells how Hezekiah showed the envoys his treasures and received a warning of exile to Babylon.

insights.title: Exalted among the nations
insights.body: After the deliverance, many brought gifts to Yahweh and Hezekiah was "exalted in the sight of all nations" (32:23). His burial "in the ascent of the tombs of the sons of David" honoured him (32:33). In Chronicles he stands with David and Solomon as a model king.

33.summary: Manasseh undoes his father's reforms and leads Judah into worse evil than the nations, but when Assyria takes him in chains to Babylon he humbles himself, is restored, and removes the idols; his son Amon does evil without repenting and is assassinated.
33.lookfor: Notice what happens to Manasseh in distress, and compare his response with his son Amon's.

names.name: Manasseh
names.gloss: Hezekiah's son, king of Judah for fifty-five years, the longest reign of any of its kings.

names.name: Baals
names.gloss: Local forms of the Canaanite storm god Baal.

names.name: valley of the son of Hinnom
names.gloss: A valley south of Jerusalem associated with child sacrifice.

names.name: Ophel
names.gloss: The ridge between the City of David and the temple mount.

names.name: Hozai
names.gloss: An otherwise unknown seer whose history the Chronicler cites; the Hebrew may simply mean "the seers."

names.name: Amon
names.gloss: Manasseh's son, king for two years before being assassinated.

names.name: Josiah
names.gloss: Amon's son, made king at eight years old.

insights.title: Worse than the nations
insights.body: Manasseh rebuilt the high places, worshipped the stars, sacrificed his children and set an idol in God's house (33:3-7). He led Judah to do "more evil than did the nations whom Yahweh destroyed" (33:9). Kings holds his sins responsible for the eventual fall of Jerusalem.

insights.title: A vassal of Assyria
insights.body: Assyrian records list Manasseh of Judah among the kings who sent tribute and materials to Esarhaddon and Ashurbanipal. Babylon was then under Assyrian control, and a revolt there in 652 to 648 BC may explain why a suspect vassal was brought to Babylon (33:11). No Assyrian text mentions the capture itself.

insights.title: Humbled in chains
insights.body: "When he was in distress, he begged Yahweh his God, and humbled himself greatly" (33:12). God heard him and brought him back to Jerusalem, "Then Manasseh knew that Yahweh was God" (33:13). Only Chronicles tells of his repentance; Kings says nothing about it.

insights.title: The Prayer of Manasseh
insights.body: The Chronicler mentions "his prayer to his God" (33:18) without giving it. A short penitential prayer attributed to Manasseh circulated in Jewish and Christian circles. Orthodox churches include it in their Bibles, while Catholic and Protestant traditions place it among the Apocrypha or in an appendix.

insights.title: Even the worst king
insights.body: If Manasseh, the worst of Judah's kings, could be forgiven and restored, then no one was beyond God's mercy. For readers in the exile's aftermath, his story was a picture of their own: sin, captivity in Babylon, repentance and return. Paul calls himself the foremost of sinners to show the extent of God's patience.

insights.title: Reform, but partial
insights.body: Manasseh removed the idols and restored Yahweh's altar, but the people still sacrificed on high places, "but only to Yahweh their God" (33:17). His late repentance could not undo all the damage of decades. His son Amon went back to the idols immediately.

insights.title: The people of the land
insights.body: "The people of the land" killed Amon's assassins and made Josiah king (33:25). The phrase often refers to the landowning citizens of Judah, who at several points stepped in to secure David's line. They had done the same for Joash and would for Jehoahaz.

insights.title: Late repentance
insights.body: Manasseh repented late, after doing great harm, and was forgiven. How do you hold together the reality of God's forgiveness and the lasting consequences of a person's actions on others?

34.summary: Josiah seeks God as a youth, purges idolatry from Judah and the north, and while the temple is being repaired the book of the law is found; after hearing it and consulting the prophetess Huldah, he leads the people in a covenant to keep it.
34.lookfor: Notice the order of Josiah's actions and his reaction when the book is read to him.

names.name: Josiah
names.gloss: King of Judah from age eight for thirty-one years, the last great reforming king.

names.name: Shaphan
names.gloss: The royal scribe whose family later supported the prophet Jeremiah.

names.name: Hilkiah
names.gloss: The high priest who found the book of the law in the temple.

names.name: Huldah
names.gloss: A prophetess in Jerusalem consulted about the book of the law.

names.name: Ahikam
names.gloss: Shaphan's son, an official who later protected Jeremiah.

names.name: Naphtali
names.gloss: A tribe in the far north, in Galilee.

insights.title: Seeking as a youth
insights.body: "In the eighth year of his reign, while he was yet young, he began to seek after the God of David" (34:3), at about sixteen. At about twenty he began to purge the land. In Chronicles, his reform starts before the book is found, while Kings tells it as a response to the book.

insights.title: Bones on the altars
insights.body: Josiah "burned the bones of the priests on their altars" (34:5). Kings tells how, generations earlier, a man of God had foretold that a king named Josiah would burn priests' bones on Jeroboam's altar at Bethel. Burning human bones defiled the altars so they could not be used again.

insights.title: Reaching into the north
insights.body: Josiah's reform extended to "the cities of Manasseh, Ephraim, and Simeon, even to Naphtali" (34:6). Assyria's power was collapsing in these years, which allowed Judah to expand northward into former Israelite territory. Josiah used the opening to reunite worship around Jerusalem.

insights.title: The book of the law
insights.body: Hilkiah "found the book of Yahweh's law given by Moses" (34:14). Since early church fathers such as Jerome, many have identified it with Deuteronomy or its core, because Josiah's reforms closely match Deuteronomy's demands, especially worship at one chosen place. Its curses explain the king's alarm (34:24).

insights.title: The second quarter
insights.body: Huldah lived "in the second quarter" (34:22), Hebrew mishneh, probably the newer district on the western hill that had grown in Hezekiah's day. Zephaniah, a contemporary, mentions the same quarter. Later tradition named the southern gates of the temple mount the Huldah Gates.

insights.title: A tender heart
insights.body: Huldah's message spares Josiah "because your heart was tender, and you humbled yourself before God" (34:27). Judgment on Jerusalem would come, but not in his days. Josiah responds not by relaxing but by gathering the people to renew the covenant (34:29-32).

insights.title: Jeremiah's young years
insights.body: Jeremiah was called in the thirteenth year of Josiah, a year after the purge began. He praised Josiah for doing justice and caring for the poor. The covenant renewal of this chapter shaped the world in which Jeremiah preached.

35.summary: Josiah celebrates a great Passover with the priests and Levites in their appointed places, unmatched since Samuel's day, but later he goes out against Pharaoh Neco at Megiddo and is fatally wounded, and all Judah mourns him.
35.lookfor: Notice how much of the Passover is organised by the Levites, and compare Josiah's last battle with Ahab's.

names.name: Neco
names.gloss: Pharaoh Necho II of Egypt, who marched north in 609 BC.

names.name: Carchemish
names.gloss: A city on the upper Euphrates, scene of major battles between Egypt, Assyria and Babylon.

names.name: Megiddo
names.gloss: A fortified city guarding a pass into the Jezreel Valley, site of many battles.

names.name: Jeremiah
names.gloss: The prophet who ministered from Josiah's reign to the fall of Jerusalem.

names.name: Jeduthun
names.gloss: A Levite musician from David's time, here called the king's seer.

insights.title: Passover in the first month
insights.body: Josiah kept Passover "on the fourteenth day of the first month" (35:1), the date set in the Law, unlike Hezekiah's second-month Passover. This time everything was in order. The Chronicler gives nineteen verses to a festival Kings describes in three.

insights.title: Put the ark in the house
insights.body: Josiah told the Levites, "Put the holy ark in the house which Solomon... built. It will no longer be a burden on your shoulders" (35:3). It is unclear whether the ark had been moved out under Manasseh or whether this is a way of saying their carrying duties were over. It is the last mention of the ark in the Old Testament's historical books.

insights.title: Roasted and boiled
insights.body: "They roasted the Passover with fire according to the ordinance" (35:13). The Hebrew literally says they boiled (bashal) the Passover in fire. Exodus forbids boiling the Passover lamb and requires roasting, while Deuteronomy uses bashal; the Chronicler's wording combines the two texts.

insights.title: Neco and Carchemish
insights.body: In 609 BC Pharaoh Neco marched north to support the remnants of Assyria against the rising Babylonians, as the Babylonian Chronicle confirms. Josiah tried to stop him at Megiddo (35:22). Four years later Babylon defeated Egypt at Carchemish, and Judah fell under Babylonian control.

insights.title: Disguised like Ahab
insights.body: Josiah "disguised himself" to fight (35:22), using the same verb as Ahab at Ramoth Gilead. Like Ahab, he was hit by archers and asked to be taken out of the battle (35:23). The Chronicler says Josiah did not listen to God's word through Neco, a surprising messenger.

insights.title: Mourning at Megiddo
insights.body: "Jeremiah lamented for Josiah," and singers remembered him in lamentations for generations (35:25). Zechariah later compared a great mourning in Jerusalem to the mourning in the valley of Megiddo. The name Armageddon in Revelation probably comes from the Hebrew for mountain of Megiddo.

insights.title: A good king's mistake
insights.body: Josiah was faithful for decades, yet died after refusing a warning he did not recognise as from God. What does his end suggest about the need to keep listening for God's word, even after a lifetime of faithfulness?

36.summary: Judah's last four kings are quickly dethroned by Egypt and Babylon, the people mock God's prophets, Jerusalem and the temple are burned and the people exiled, until Cyrus of Persia proclaims that God's people may go up to rebuild.
36.lookfor: Notice how quickly the end comes, the reason given for the exile, and the note on which the book ends.

names.name: Jehoahaz
names.gloss: Josiah's son, king for three months before being taken to Egypt.

names.name: Jehoiakim
names.gloss: Josiah's son, renamed by Pharaoh, king for eleven years.

names.name: Nebuchadnezzar
names.gloss: King of Babylon 605 to 562 BC, who destroyed Jerusalem.

names.name: Jehoiachin
names.gloss: Jehoiakim's son, taken to Babylon after a reign of three months.

names.name: Zedekiah
names.gloss: The last king of Judah, installed by Nebuchadnezzar.

names.name: Chaldeans
names.gloss: The people of southern Mesopotamia whose dynasty ruled Babylon.

names.name: Cyrus
names.gloss: King of Persia who conquered Babylon in 539 BC and allowed exiles to return.

insights.title: Until there was no remedy
insights.body: God "sent to them by his messengers, rising up early and sending, because he had compassion," but "they mocked the messengers of God... until there was no remedy" (36:15-16). The Hebrew word for remedy is related to healing. The healing promised in 7:14 to a repentant people was refused.

insights.title: Four kings, quickly
insights.body: Jehoahaz, Jehoiakim, Jehoiachin and Zedekiah reign in twenty-one verses. Each is removed by a foreign king, and the temple vessels go to Babylon in stages (36:7, 36:10, 36:18). Some details differ from Kings: Kings makes Jehoiachin eighteen when he began to reign, not eight (36:9).

insights.title: An oath broken
insights.body: Zedekiah rebelled against Nebuchadnezzar, "who had made him swear by God" (36:13). Ezekiel condemns this as breaking an oath made in God's name. The king "didn't humble himself before Jeremiah the prophet" (36:12), whose warnings fill the book of Jeremiah.

insights.title: The land's Sabbaths
insights.body: The exile lasted "until the land had enjoyed its Sabbaths" (36:21). The Law required the land to rest every seventh year, and Leviticus warned that if Israel ignored it, the land would rest while they were in exile. Jeremiah's seventy years and the neglected Sabbath years are combined here.

insights.title: Cyrus's decree
insights.body: In 539 BC Cyrus conquered Babylon. His clay cylinder, found in 1879, describes his policy of returning displaced peoples and restoring their sanctuaries, though it does not mention the Jews. The decree in 36:22-23 matches that policy and is repeated at the start of Ezra.

insights.title: Let him go up
insights.body: In the Jewish order of the Hebrew Bible, Chronicles is the last book, so the whole Scripture ends with Cyrus's words: "let him go up" (36:23). The Hebrew verb, alah, gives the word aliyah, still used for going up to Jerusalem. The story of exile closes on an invitation to return and rebuild.

insights.title: Fire in the sanctuary
insights.body: The Chaldeans killed young men "in the house of their sanctuary" and burned God's house (36:17, 36:19). The temple where God's glory had filled the house and fire had fallen on the altar was itself consumed. The warning given to Solomon in 7:19-22 came true.

insights.title: An ending that is a beginning
insights.body: The Chronicler could have ended with the burning of the temple, but chose to end with the decree to rebuild. What does it say about God and about his people that the story of judgment closes with an invitation?

intro.who: Jewish tradition in the Talmud credits Ezra with writing Chronicles, which was originally one book with 1 Chronicles. Most modern scholars speak of an anonymous "Chronicler," probably from Levite or temple circles in Jerusalem, and they debate whether the same hand also shaped Ezra and Nehemiah.
intro.when: It covers Solomon's reign (from about 970 BC) to the fall of Jerusalem in 586 BC and ends with Cyrus's decree of 539 BC. Most scholars date its writing to the Persian period, around 400 to 350 BC.
intro.why: It retells the story of Judah's kings for the community rebuilt after the exile, measuring each king by whether he sought God and cared for the temple, and it ends with an invitation to go up and rebuild.
